extracted.intended_audience: writers, orators, and literary critics seeking to produce or evaluate sublime/lofty style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing and judging 'the Sublime' in poetry, prose, and oratory: identifies sources of sublimity, faults to avoid, and practical stylistic distinctions (e.g., amplification vs. sublimity). Intended as a prescriptive rhetorical manual for elevated writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sublime consists in a certain loftiness and excellence of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Sublime is not mere persuasion or arrangement but a quality of language that gives a writer lasting eminence; it lifts readers out of themselves and exerts an imperious and irresistible force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime's effect on the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: A lofty passage does not convince the reason of the reader, but takes him out of himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublimity acts with irresistible force, swaying every reader whether he will or no; it can illumine an entire subject 'like a lightning-flash' and seize attention and memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of language as prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: All five sources of sublimity presuppose the preliminary gift of command of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without solid linguistic command, the other sources (grandeur of thought, passions, figures, dignified expression, structure) cannot produce true sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandeur of thought (first and most important source)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grandeur of thought: a certain lofty cast of mind or lofty conception is the most important source of the Sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublime thoughts belong to generous, aspiring minds; the author should cultivate noble and majestic ideas (training the soul) because a great thought can be sublime even unuttered (example: Homeric silence of Ajax).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vigorous and spirited treatment of the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: A vigorous and spirited treatment of the passions is a principal source of sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate, genuine passion—'divine inspiration' or 'fine madness'—can be highly conducive to sublimity, but note that not all passions are lofty (pity, grief, fear can be low), so pathos is not identical with sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artifice in the employment of figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of figures (both figures of thought and figures of speech) is a source of sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures must be used artfully; they can assist sublimity but are not sufficient alone. Distinguish between helpful metaphors and mere high-flown conceits that become ludicrous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignified expression (choice of words and metaphors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dignified expression: proper choice of words and use of metaphors and other ornaments of diction contribute to sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the most fitting, elevated words and metaphors; avoid frigid or paltry diction. Metaphors should dignify, not degrade, the subject (avoid incongruous or ludicrous images).

rubrics_metrics.name: Majesty and elevation of structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Majesty and elevation of structure (including arrangement and compositional grandeur) is a source that embraces and enhances the other causes of sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lofty structural plan—amplification used properly, powerful climaxes, unified arrangement—helps sustain the effect of sublimity across a passage or work.

rubrics_metrics.name: True vs. False Sublimity (criteria for authenticity)
rubrics_metrics.description: True Sublimity is sustained, pregnant in suggestion, hard to distract from, and takes strong and lasting hold on the memory; false sublimity is a specious exterior hiding emptiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test by repeated reading and by reading across different cultivated critics: if the work fails to produce lofty ideas on repeated judgment or fades from memory, it is not truly sublime. True sublime 'always please and please all readers' across differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of bombast (overblown grandiloquence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bombast is hollow, affected bulk that transcends the Sublime and becomes objectionable or burlesque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambitious writers often, to avoid appearing weak, swell into the opposite extreme; avoid inflated phrases (examples: 'curling torrent flames', 'vomiting to heaven') that produce confusion, absurdity, or ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of puerility (over-elaboration and frigidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Puerility is the failing of feeble minds—pedantic over-elaboration that ends in frigidity and paltriness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-polish or gild trivial thought; polish aimed at mere attractiveness can lead to silliness and loss of grandeur. The avoidance of puerility preserves dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of false sentiment (ill-timed or empty emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: False sentiment is an ill-timed and empty display of emotion where no emotion is called for, or of greater emotion than warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid tedious displays of personal feeling disconnected from subject; excessive or inappropriate pathos leaves readers cold and undermines sublimity. This topic merits separate treatment when handling the pathetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of frigidity in striving for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Frigidity arises when a writer, eager to seem striking and novel, produces childish absurdities or over-ingenious conceits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty for its own sake often produces ludicrous images and mistakes in taste (examples cited from Timaeus, Xenophon, Plato). Prefer natural dignity over contrived cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and combination of striking circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: One cause of sublimity is the choice of the most striking circumstances in what is described and the power of combining them into one animate whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick the vivid, essential features and weld them together; reject anything frivolous, unbecoming, or tiresome. Examples: Sappho and Homer choose vivid, contradictory tokens to convey tumult; avoid diluting terror with ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and emphasis: reject non-essential detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Great writers fastidiously reject whatever is not essential; interposition of frivolous details mars sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against the introduction of anything that weakens the main impression; avoid patching an edifice of sublimity with irrelevant or decorative fragments that cause a 'patched and gaping' effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplification distinct from Sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplification is the gathering together and repeated insistence on all constituent parts of a subject to give extension; sublimity gives elevation while amplification gives extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amplification requires diffusiveness and prolixity and without sublimity becomes lifeless; use amplification when you need progressive, ascending points, perorations, or widespread effect, but supply it with sublimity (soul) to be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate style choice (sudden vs. diffusive sublimity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different modes of sublimity suit different purposes: the high-strung, abrupt sublimity of Demosthenes vs. the diffused, extended sublimity of Cicero or Plato.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use abrupt, vehement style when wanting to exaggerate or rouse vehement emotion; use the diffusive, rolling style for perorations, familiar topics, descriptions, digressions, and long overpowering effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of great models (not plagiarism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emulous imitation of great poets and prose-writers is a legitimate path to sublimity—'not plagiarism, but resembling the process of copying from fair forms.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn by imitating Homer, Plato, Demosthenes, Thucydides, etc.; draw inspiration from predecessors' genius to acquire an 'effluence' of grandeur, while avoiding simple copying of phrases (plagiarism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/decency limits on grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimity must respect decency and proportion: descriptions that are impious or degrade subjects (e.g., gods) overstep proper bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid images or combinations that, while intended to be vast, become impious or indecorous (example: 'Battle of the Gods' made grotesque); sublimity should elevate without violating taste or decency.
